# A guide to the book {.unnumbered}

::: {.hero}
**QUANTUM MANY-BODY DYNAMICS**

## What does a quantum system forget—and what does it keep?

A density matrix describes every measurement on a subsystem whose environment
has been ignored. Yet the same density matrix can hide very different
distributions of conditional wavefunctions, different histories, and different
resources. This book develops the tools needed to see that additional structure.
:::

![One physical evolution can be examined through several different information
structures. Each arrow specifies what is sampled or retained; none is an
automatic implication between different notions of randomness. Original diagram.](figs/concept-map.svg)

## Purpose and prerequisites

This is a graduate introduction to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics through
ensembles, information, and constraints. It starts with complex vectors and
probabilities and proceeds to current questions about deep thermalization,
Hilbert-space ergodicity, quantum resources, dynamical maps, and temporal
memory. The intended reader has encountered elementary quantum mechanics and
linear algebra. No previous course in quantum information or statistical
mechanics is assumed. The mathematical appendix reviews the specific tools
used in the derivations.

The scientific backbone is recent work by Wen Wei Ho and collaborators,
especially papers from 2024–2026, together with the foundational literature
needed to understand it. The organizing principles are physical questions.
This is an independent educational synthesis, not an authorized account of a
research group. Exposition and figures are original and AI-assisted. Literature
coverage is current through **20 October 2026**.

## The main ideas

Ordinary thermalization asks whether a small subsystem's density matrix becomes
thermal. Deep thermalization asks a more detailed question: after measuring
the surrounding bath, how are the subsystem's conditional states distributed?
The first moment of this distribution is the density matrix. Its higher
moments reveal information that averaging has removed.

Hilbert-space ergodicity instead samples a trajectory at different times.
Although its mathematics also uses moments of quantum states, its sampling
protocol and obstructions differ. Static unitary dynamics preserves populations
in its energy basis. An aperiodic drive may remove this obstruction, while
taking extraordinarily long to become ergodic.

Quantum resource theories ask which kinds of useful structure remain under a
specified class of operations. Coherence, magic, and entanglement are different
resources. Their fluctuations can distinguish phases whose mean density
matrices agree. Quantum channels and multi-time processes then extend the
discussion from distributions of states to distributions of transformations
and patterns of memory.

Finally, constrained dynamics shows why universal randomness is conditional.
Scars, disconnected dynamical sectors, conservation laws, and high-frequency
driving can all restrict the states that are explored. The right equilibrium
benchmark must respect those restrictions.

## How to read

The full route is sequential. A first reading can follow one of these paths:

| Interest | Suggested path |
|---|---|
| First encounter with the subject | Foundations → projected ensembles → temporal ergodicity |
| Deep thermalization | Foundations → projected ensembles → Scrooge ensembles → resource transitions |
| Driven dynamics | Thermalization → temporal ergodicity → aperiodic drives → driven phases |
| Open systems and simulation | States and measurement → channels → temporal entanglement → laboratory |
| Constraints and experiments | Thermalization → scars and fragmentation → driven phases → laboratory |

Every chapter supplies worked examples and exercises. Hints help with the
first step; selected complete solutions appear in the solutions appendix.
Exercises labelled “research” are proposals for investigation and may have
no established answer. The computational laboratory uses Julia and only its
standard libraries, so every numerical illustration can be regenerated.

## Conventions and claims

We use $\hbar=1$. A state vector is normalized unless explicitly called
unnormalized. Subsystems are $A,B,\ldots$, their Hilbert-space dimensions are
$d_A,d_B,\ldots$, and $k$ is a moment order. The trace distance is
$D(\rho,\sigma)=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$. Entropies use natural logarithms,
except when a result is explicitly expressed in bits. The Haar ensemble is
complex unless a real ensemble is explicitly specified.

An **identity** follows from the definitions. A **theorem** has stated
hypotheses, which matter. A **model result** need not apply to all dynamics.
**Numerical evidence** is limited by size and time. A **conjecture** or
**open question** is not presented as established physics. In particular,
agreement with a few moments is not a proof of all-order randomness, and a
finite-time plateau is not a proof of an asymptotic phase.

The research program's broad context is surveyed in @ergMark2026.
The [annotated literature guide](c-literature-guide.qmd) provides a route from
the derivations here to the primary sources.
